In contrast, our NLI-based approach using DeBERTa-v3-large (approx. 400M parameters) achieved a final evaluation F1 score of \textbf{0.81}. This demonstrates that for the specific task of clarity detection, framing the problem as logical entailment is significantly more effective and computationally efficient than fine-tuning massive generative models. However, for Subtask 2 (Evasion Techniques), the researchers' baseline (0.51) outperformed our best MIL approach \textbf{0.45}. This suggests that identifying fine-grained linguistic nuances (e.g., distinguishing ``Deflection" from ``Dodging") benefits from the vast world knowledge and reasoning capabilities embedded in 70B+ parameter models, which smaller discriminative models struggle to capture fully. \subsection{Performance Analysis} \subsubsection{Context vs. Segmentation in Evasion} For Subtask 2, the Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) approach outperformed ModernBERT (0.46 vs. 0.38). While ModernBERT captures the entire context (8192 tokens), the ``evasion" label is often localized. The global pooling of ModernBERT may dilute these specific signals. In contrast, the Attention Pooling mechanism in MIL explicitly assigns high weights to the most discriminative segments of the answer, effectively isolating the evasion tactic. \subsubsection{The Trade-off of Hierarchical Constraints} While the Multi-Task Hierarchical Gating (MTL) and Hierarchy-Aware Global Model (HiAGM) were designed to explicitly model the taxonomic dependencies described in Section 4.6 and 4.7 , they achieved lower Macro-F1 scores (0.64 and 0.52 respectively) on Subtask 1 compared to the NLI approach. We observe that the Hierarchical Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{cons}$) and the post-hoc deterministic inference used in HiAGM may have been overly restrictive. By forcing the model to strictly adhere to the parent-child relationship, we likely introduced a "bottleneck" where errors in fine-grained evasion detection (Subtask 2) propagated upward, penalizing the clarity prediction (Subtask 1). In contrast, the NLI model's flexibility to treat clarity as a logical entailment problem allowed for better generalization across varied presidential rhetorical styles. \subsubsection{The Generative Lag} Our generative approach (\texttt{Llama-3.2-3B}) underperformed, achieving only 0.57 F1. This reinforces our finding that without the massive scale of the researchers' $70\text{B}$ model, generative decoding is less stable than discriminative classification for this task. \subsubsection{Inefficacy of Augmentation} Contrary to our hypothesis, the data augmentation strategies described in Section 4.8 did not yield statistically significant improvements in Macro-F1 scores for either Subtask 1 or Subtask 2, with performance remaining stagnant or declining. We attribute this to the \textit{fragility of political nuance}. Political evasion depends on subtle rhetorical cues (e.g., ``shifting'' or ``flouting Gricean Maxims''), making class boundaries highly sensitive to perturbations. This is consistent with \citet{b4}, who reported low inter-annotator agreement ($\kappa = 0.48$) and difficulty distinguishing semantically proximate categories such as \textit{General} and \textit{Implicit}.
